case.label: D
case.text: D also gets encrypted copies out of the production account with a customer managed key, and it satisfies 'a copy of each snapshot in a separate account'. A hurried reader could call it a superset of A that adds redundancy. It fails the MOST secure test because it shares the key and copies with every account in the organization, not only the isolated backup account, and the stem names one backup account. The word MOST and 'isolated' make A the only option that limits the sharing to the one account. B and C fail on a hard rule (an AWS managed key cannot be shared or have its policy edited), so they are weaker cases than D.

case.label: E
case.text: E is the tempting wrong pick: a single shared volume, formatted with a common file system, mounted on both nodes looks like the simplest way to give both nodes the same data with the least work. It fails because XFS is not cluster-aware, so two nodes writing at once corrupt it, and the stem says the application does not coordinate writes. B (gp3) is the second weak case: Multi-Attach is documented for io1 and io2 only, so B fails. C is a valid but high-overhead design, which the LEAST operational overhead wording rules out. The pair A and D is the one set that works and needs no new code.

answers.flag: D (gp3) also meets 60 MiB/s with its included baseline, so B wins only on price per GB, which the stem does not state; B's phrase 'sized so that its throughput matches the reads and writes that the workload performs each day' is also muddled (st1 throughput scales with volume size, not with daily volume), so a careful candidate could read B as a wrong sizing rule and pick D.

case.label: D
case.text: D meets every stated constraint. gp3 includes a baseline throughput above 60 MiB/s, so no extra provisioning is needed, and the option says to provision above baseline only as needed, so it adds no waste. gp3 also gives steady performance with no burst bucket, which fits 'sustained from start to end' and 'must finish each scan quickly'. The stem gives no prices, so 'MOST cost-effective' cannot be settled from the stem alone. B's text sizes the volume by 'reads and writes each day', which is a daily-volume rule and not a sustained-rate rule, so a reader can judge B as badly specified and prefer D as the safe, well-specified choice. A candidate can also doubt whether st1 holds 60 MiB/s for a full scan: at 2 TiB its baseline is 80 MiB/s, which is enough, but the stem does not tell the candidate this and the burst-bucket concept adds doubt. The cue 'large files sequentially' plus the sc1 distractor 'lowest price per GB' points toward st1, so the wording also gives the answer away to a pattern-matcher.

case.label: A
case.text: A is the cheapest on paper: instance store volumes cost nothing beyond the instance price, and they give very high IOPS for small random I/O, far above 2,000. A reader could say the files are 'working files' that are rebuilt, so losing them is acceptable. It fails because the stem requires the files to survive a stop and start, and instance store data does not survive a stop. C is a weaker case: it meets the IOPS but costs more than D. B fails on IOPS because sc1 is built for throughput, not for 2,000 small random operations. The explicit 'stopped and started again' is a strong cue, but it is a stated requirement and not a giveaway.
